metadata.note: Illinois Central's Iowa Division: Chicago (via Freeport) to Dubuque, then west across Iowa through Iowa Falls and Fort Dodge to Sioux City, plus a branch from Cherokee north-west to Sioux Falls, SD. Built by predecessor companies (Dubuque and Pacific Railroad; Dubuque and Sioux City Railroad) and leased/absorbed by the Illinois Central starting Oct 1 1867. This was IC's major western reach, independent of and complementary to the Chicago-New Orleans main line (see illinois_central.geojson). GEOMETRY METHODOLOGY: the Chicago-Dubuque-Iowa Falls-Fort Dodge-Sioux City main line (837.4 km / 520.4 mi) is real-traced through OpenStreetMap active-rail data (Overpass API, shortest-path graph search) -- still active trackage today (Canadian National, which acquired IC in 1998-99). The Cherokee-Sioux Falls branch was re-traced on 2026-08-27: it had been three hand-placed waypoints drawing an 84.3-mile straight line on the wrong alignment (west-north-west direct to Sioux Falls), which is not where the branch ran. The grade IS mapped in OSM, as abandoned and razed ways, but mostly untagged - the earlier attempt looked for IC-tagged ways and found none connected. Routing over abandoned/razed geometry with foreign-operator ways weighted out now gives 95.7 mi against 96.7 documented, on the real route via Larrabee, Primghar, Sheldon and Rock Rapids and across the south-west tip of Minnesota.

segments.note: Built in 1887 by the Cherokee & Dakota Railroad, incorporated 15 July 1887 and constructed in about six months; the last spike went in on the evening of 19 December 1887 and Sioux Falls turned out with the Damon Division Band to meet its fourth railroad. The line became an Illinois Central branch shortly afterwards and is drawn in IC colours throughout. The quartzite passenger depot at the Big Sioux River and 8th Street opened in 1888. DATE CONFLICT: some secondary sources (dbpedia, and this file before 2026-08-27) give 1877 for this branch; the contemporary newspaper record behind the depot's National Register nomination puts the arrival at 19 December 1887, and that date is used here. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 19 December 1887 arrival, the 1887-88 depot and the Cherokee & Dakota Railroad's role are from the NRHP nomination for the Illinois Central Passenger Depot in Sioux Falls, the Wikipedia article on that depot, and the Cherokee historical photo caption; the headway is an estimate and is not sourced.

segments.note: Decline on a 96.7-mile country branch. The Sioux Falls depot was converted to freight use after passenger traffic fell away in the 1950s, which is the only dating available for the end of passenger service; 1955 is an editorial midpoint, NOT a documented last-train date. Freight lasted much longer - the branch survived under Illinois Central Gulf until heavy rain took out the Big Sioux River trestle and it was abandoned in 1984 - but that is context, not drawn service (Rule 1). Frequency estimated.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: 'passenger traffic fell off in the 1950s' (Dakota News Now, historic-structures.com, both following the NRHP nomination) is the only evidence for the end year, and 1955 is an editorial reading of it. The 1930 split and the headway are estimates. The 1984 abandonment is sourced.

properties.geometry_quality: real-traced from OpenStreetMap, replacing three hand-placed waypoints. The corridor is followed as mapped abandoned and razed grade from Cherokee north-west through Larrabee, Primghar, Sheldon and Rock Rapids, across the extreme south-west corner of Rock County, Minnesota, to Rowena (East Sioux Falls). 95.7 mi traced against 96.7 mi documented. Only IC-tagged and untagged abandoned grade was used - ways tagged to other operators were weighted out of the routing - and 1.4 mi of small connector bridges (longest 0.45 mi) fill gaps where the grade is unmapped. One deliberate straight-line approximation: the final 1.5 mi from the end of the mapped grade east of the Big Sioux into the depot site at 8th Street, where the alignment and the river trestle are gone.
